title: Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan Sign Makkah Defence Pact; Ukraine Strikes Two Russian Refineries; Iran Confirms Hormuz Framework With Oman
subhead: A new Sunni defence pact reshapes Gulf security calculations just as Iran and Oman confirm a Hormuz framework deal that Tehran says won't fully reopen the strait. Ukraine drones hit two Russian refineries and shadow fleet vessels, while European gas storage sits at its lowest since 2011.

sections.heading: Makkah Joint Defence Agreement: A New Sunni Security Architecture
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on Friday, August 7, stipulating that an armed attack on any of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against all. The pact was signed in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, according to AP, CBS News, and identical statements from the Pakistani Foreign Ministry and Turkey's presidential communications directorate.

A Turkish government official, speaking on condition of anonymity, described the agreement as 'purely defensive in nature' and insisted the deal is 'not against any specific actor,' adding it is open for other regional countries to join. Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said the pact 'does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc' and is 'focused on building sustainable capabilities.' Turkish media reported the agreement likely covers joint military exercises, technology transfers, and intelligence sharing.

The pact builds on the bilateral Pakistan-Saudi mutual defence pact signed in September 2025, which already defined an attack on either nation as an attack on both. Pakistan contributes nuclear capability, Turkey brings NATO's second-largest army and a growing defence industry, and Saudi Arabia provides oil wealth and Gulf strategic position. Al-Monitor notes the pact is being watched closely as a potential deterrent against Iran, even though signatories publicly avoid naming Tehran. Iran's state media mocked the agreement as insufficient to bring Riyadh security.

Jewish Insider reports that US national security experts have expressed concern about the pact's implications — particularly the prospect of a mutual defence obligation tying Washington to three allies simultaneously, two of whom (Turkey and Pakistan) have complicated relations with both Iran and each other.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first formal three-way defence pact among major Sunni powers that explicitly links an attack on one to a response by all — a qualitative shift from bilateral security understandings. It creates a new security bloc alongside (and potentially in tension with) the US security umbrella in the Gulf.

sections.heading: Iran Confirms Hormuz Framework Deal; Seeks to Bar US and Israeli Vessels
sections.body:
Iran confirmed on August 8 that a framework agreement with Oman on managing Strait of Hormuz transit has been reached, with final details to be announced soon, according to Iran's foreign ministry and Moneycontrol. A US official told Reuters on August 7 that 'there is progress between Oman and Iran on the strait, and we expect a deal soon,' adding that once a deal is announced to restore commercial shipping without impediments, 'the United States will lift the blockade of Iranian ports.'

But crucial caveats emerged. Republic World and MSN report that Iran is seeking to bar US and Israeli shipping vessels from the Hormuz arrangement — a condition that would severely limit the deal's scope if accepted. Separately, Iran stated that the agreement 'won't fully reopen the strait,' per MSN, suggesting Tehran intends to retain leverage over transits even after a deal is signed. The Trump administration has ruled out any arrangement that cements Iran's grip on the waterway, including fee collection, according to earlier reporting.

Abu Dhabi National Oil Company said on August 7 that 15 of its vessels have been struck in what it called unprovoked attacks while transiting the strait since the conflict began, killing one crew member and wounding 20. The Hindu notes that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian defended diplomacy on state television, telling hardliners: 'When we can get our rights through dialogue, why not do it?' — a rare public signal of internal divisions between Iran's civilian leadership and hardline power centers around Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei and the IRGC.
sections.whyItMatters: A Hormuz framework exists on paper but the gap between what Iran calls a deal and what the US would accept remains vast — Iran wants to exclude US/Israeli shipping and retain transit controls, while Washington demands unconditional reopening. The internal Iranian debate between Pezeshkian's camp and hardliners may determine whether this framework becomes operational or collapses again.

sections.heading: Ukraine Drones Hit Two Russian Refineries and Shadow Fleet Vessels
sections.body:
Ukraine struck two Russian oil refineries in a coordinated long-range drone attack on August 6-7, according to the Kyiv Independent and United24 Media. The targets were the Slavneft-Yanos refinery in Yaroslavl and the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Bashkortostan — both deep inside Russia, roughly 800-1,200 km from the front lines. President Zelensky confirmed the strikes, calling them part of Ukraine's continued effort to degrade Russia's energy revenue base.

United24 Media reports that Ukraine also struck Russian patrol boats and shadow fleet vessels in the same operation. The shadow fleet — a loose network of ageing, uninsured tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions on Russian oil — has been a key enabler of Moscow's export revenue. Hitting these vessels directly marks an escalation from Ukraine's previous focus on refinery infrastructure alone.

The Yaroslavl and Bashkortostan strikes demonstrate that Ukraine's drone reach now extends across most of European Russia, including regions previously considered safe from attack. Both facilities are significant: Slavneft-Yanos processes approximately 18 million tonnes of crude annually, while Bashneft-Novoil is a major supplier of refined products to the Russian domestic market and military logistics chain.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine is now systematically targeting both the production side (refineries) and the export side (shadow fleet vessels) of Russia's oil revenue machine. The shadow fleet strikes, if sustained, could be more consequential than refinery hits — they threaten the sanctions-evasion infrastructure that keeps Russian oil flowing to global markets.

sections.heading: European Gas Storage at Lowest Since 2011 as Winter Approaches
sections.body:
European gas storage has fallen to 57% capacity, the lowest level since 2011 for this time of year, according to OilPrice citing Gas Infrastructure Europe data. The figure is roughly 15 percentage points below the 5-year average and well under the EU's 90% November 1 fill target mandated under regulation.

The shortfall is driven by reduced Russian pipeline flows, disrupted LNG supply chains due to the Hormuz crisis redirecting Middle Eastern cargoes, and increased summer cooling demand across Southern Europe. The combination means Europe enters the 2026-27 heating season with a thinner buffer than at any point since the pre-storage-expansion era.

OilPrice reports that front-month TTF Dutch gas futures have climbed above EUR 48/MWh, with winter contracts trading above EUR 55/MWh — still well below the 2022 crisis peak of over EUR 300/MWh, but a sharp increase from the sub-EUR 30 levels seen in early 2025. Analysts note that a cold winter combined with continued Hormuz disruption could push prices to levels that restart demand destruction in industry.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is heading into winter with its thinnest gas cushion in 15 years, and the Hormuz crisis means the usual LNG safety valve may not be available. If the Iran-Oman framework doesn't restore tanker traffic quickly, the EU's 90% fill target will be missed by a wide margin — making demand rationing likely in a cold scenario.

sections.heading: Oil Rallies on Hormuz Uncertainty But Posts Worst Weekly Decline in Months
sections.body:
Brent crude topped $83/barrel on Friday amid volatile trading driven by Hormuz deal headlines, but settled around $78.2/barrel according to Trading Economics data — posting a weekly decline exceeding 7%, one of the steepest drops in months. WTI traded near $79/barrel intraday before settling lower. The ZeeBiz report on the weekly decline attributed the sell-off to demand concerns and expectations that a Hormuz deal would eventually restore supply.

OilPrice reports that Hormuz tanker traffic has stalled to a two-month low as attacks on shipping escalated, with ADNOC confirming 15 vessel strikes. The disconnect between intraday spikes (driven by geopolitical risk premiums from the Makkah pact and Hormuz deal uncertainty) and the weekly trend (driven by demand weakness and deal optimism) illustrates a market pulled in two directions.

The ZeeBiz analysis notes that even a partial Hormuz reopening — which Iran now says is all it will offer — would likely bring a significant volume of Gulf crude back to market, pressuring prices further. But until tankers actually move safely through the strait, the risk premium remains embedded.
sections.whyItMatters: The oil market is pricing in both a near-term risk premium from Hormuz disruption and a medium-term supply recovery if a deal holds — creating unusual volatility. The 7% weekly drop despite daily headline spikes suggests traders are positioning for a deal that restores flows, while the intraday rallies show how quickly that calculus could reverse.

sections.heading: US Critical Minerals Export Restrictions Take Shape
sections.body:
The US critical minerals export restriction directive, reported earlier this week, is drawing increased attention as details emerge. The directive targets recycled critical minerals — including lithium, cobalt, and rare earths — restricting their export to prevent American-processed materials from flowing to strategic competitors, primarily China.

Forbes reported on July 30 that the restrictions are part of a broader shift toward treating minerals processing as a national security function, not just a trade policy. The CFR analysis published August 6 describes the approach as 'the shareholder state' — an improvised bet in which Washington takes equity stakes and export-control authority over critical mineral supply chains, treating them as strategic assets akin to semiconductor technology.

The directive affects recycled and secondary minerals specifically because these represent a growing and increasingly important supply stream: recycled lithium-ion batteries alone could supply 10-15% of global lithium demand by 2030, per IEA estimates cited in the Forbes analysis. Restricting their export aims to keep domestically processed materials within US-allied supply chains.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is expanding the critical minerals toolkit beyond mining subsidies into outright export controls on processed and recycled materials — effectively treating refined minerals like a controlled technology. If other processing nations follow suit, the global minerals trade fragments into blocs, with significant implications for battery and EV supply chains.

bottomLine: August 8 brought three overlapping security shifts: the Makkah Defence Pact creates a new Sunni bloc with mutual defence obligations that complicates any Hormuz resolution; Iran confirmed a Hormuz framework with Oman but immediately signaled it won't fully reopen the strait and wants US and Israeli ships excluded; and Ukraine expanded its targeting from Russian refineries to shadow fleet vessels, threatening the export side of Moscow's oil revenue. Meanwhile, European gas storage at 57% — the lowest since 2011 — makes the Hormuz standoff an acute winter supply crisis, not just a shipping disruption. Oil markets are torn between deal optimism and risk premiums, posting a 7% weekly decline despite daily intraday spikes above $83.
